title: Mother demands answers, weeks after black woman found hanging from Mississippi tree
description: The mother of a black woman whose body was found hanging from a tree in Jackson, Mississippi, has told the BBC she is still waiting for answers from o
body: The mother of a black woman whose body was found hanging from a tree in Jackson, Mississippi, has told the BBC she is still waiting for answers from officials more than a month later.Her demands have been echoed by a community in the southern US state that has been left shocked and angry.After weeks of silence, police on Tuesday confirmed for the first time that they were investigating the death of Tasia Fortune, 29, as a potential homicide - while clarifying that her official cause of death has yet to be confirmed.Authorities discovered Fortune's body on 3 August, hanging from a tree in the lot of an abandoned home.Local concern over her death has been heightened by the fact that the state has a dark history of racial violence and lynchings.The majority-black city has been left on edge. As the question lingers as to how Fortune died, petitions online signed by tens of thousands of people have called for more transparency, and members of US Congress have asked for federal intervention."It's making me angry," Fortune's mother, Christy Spivey, said. "What is the hold up?"Spivey described desperate attempts to understand the status of the investigation and how multiple enquiries to police had gone unanswered.The first update she had received from authorities in weeks came in a public city meeting on Tuesday evening as Jackson Police Chief RaShall Brackney discussed the case and said the department "has been investigating this case from day one as a homicide".Brackney, in a statement to the BBC, elaborated and said the department always treats any pending death case as a "potential homicide" so that crucial evidence is not lost as police wait on autopsy results.The department, though, had only previously described the case as a death investigation.Tuesday's statement from Brackney said "we are conducting the investigation at the highest appropriate level while we await the medical examiner's findings", which would include an official cause and manner of death.The medical examiner's office said it would not comment on the pending case.Spivey last saw her daughter alive on 26 July, when Fortune had travelled from Mississippi, where she had lived for roughly the last decade, to Kentucky, where Spivey lives, for a family reunion.The next time she saw her daughter - in a funeral home, days before her burial - she could barely look at her body."I didn't look straight at her. Her daddy did," she said. "I kind of looked from the side."Spivey remembered their last conversation. "She was talking about, you know, maybe even coming home," she explained.Fortune's death has left the community concerned that racial violence in Mississippi could be on the rise again. And in the absence of concrete details about the case, their suspicions are left to fester.Fortune's death was the third incident in Mississippi in less than a year where police found someone dead and hanged from a tree.The other two bodies - one black male, one white - were discovered in September 2025, on the exact same day.Both were ruled a suicide, though the mother of one of the deceased - Trey Reed - contests those findings.Fed-up residents have launched an online petition, which has gathered more than 50,000 signatures, for an independent investigation into the state's chief medical examiner, Dr Staci Turner, over the handling of a recent spate of cases involving people of colour. Another petition asks for the FBI to launch an investigation into Fortune's deathThe BBC has asked Turner for comment.Jackson City Councilman Kenneth Stokes has also expressed concerns about the police investigation, saying he'd been outside the home where Fortune was thought to have lived multiple times and has never seen officers."All cases are important, but this one - a hanging in Mississippi - should rise to the top of the food chain," Stokes said.He told the BBC he sent letters to both federal prosecutors at the Mississippi US attorney's office and the FBI weeks ago, urging that the investigation was "in dire need of assistance". He has yet to hear back from either."Nothing from nobody," Stokes said. "It's like nobody cares."The BBC has reached out to the Mississippi US attorney's office and the local FBI office for comment.US Congresswoman Jasmine Crockett has similarly requested federal intervention. In a letter to the US Department of Justice, she asked for an investigation into recent deaths in Mississippi - including that of Tasia Fortune - calling them "possible cases of modern-day lynchings". She cited the state's "appalling historical reputation of violent terrorism against black Americans".In addition to Mississippi, there have been multiple other cases nationally of black Americans found hanged from trees, including four in North Carolina this year alone. Three were ruled a suicide. An autopsy is pending for the fourth death.The BBC has reached out to the justice department for comment.Stokes is clear that he does not know whether Fortune's death was a lynching, or whether race played a part at all. Nor does he care. He just wants answers.Brandon King, president of the student National Association for the Advancement of Colored People (NAACP) chapter at nearby Jackson State University, said the mystery of Fortune's death, combined with minimal updates from police, has led him and others to be "extra cautious" around campus.The feeling, King said, was that "hey, you could be next. This is in Jackson. This is in your backyard".The thought is extra worrying, he continued, because "this is supposed to be the capital. This is where I'm supposed to feel the most safe".As for Spivey, she cried before heading to a funeral home for her daughter, dreading having to fill out a death certificate and decide whether to cremate or bury her firstborn child.She wanted to cremate her daughter but decided, in the end, for a burial. She said she was holding out hope there would be updates in the investigation, which might mean needing to exhume her corpse.

schema.headline: Mother demands answers, weeks after black woman found hanging from Mississippi tree

title: Uganda pulling out of Prince Harry's Invictus Games
description: The Ugandan military chief's announcement follows a letter sent this week on behalf of the King which made clear that Prince Harry and Meghan, who hav
body: The Ugandan military chief's announcement follows a letter sent this week on behalf of the King which made clear that Prince Harry and Meghan, who have now returned to the UK, were not working royals.A report in The Times newspaper quoted the general's concerns about the "Harry-Meghan nonsense", suggesting this was the background to the decision."In order not to be construed as being opposed to His Majesty King Charles III of the United Kingdom, whom we deeply revere, Uganda hereby withdraws from the Invictus Games," said the general in an overnight post."We shall not participate in anything that does not have His Majesty's approval."However, royal sources have said that the King encourages all projects which support wounded service personnel.A spokesman for the Invictus Games said they had not received any official information about a potential withdrawal and have been seeking clarification from their contacts in Uganda.Among other posts on X from General Kainerugaba on Thursday was one that read: "I consider myself the most handsome, most daring and glorious Commander who ever lived."There was also a series of angry messages about other generals who had danced without his permission.The participation of Uganda in the next games, to be held next year in Birmingham, was announced in July, when Prince Harry was in London promoting the sports event, which celebrates the resilience and rehabilitation of wounded military men and women.Uganda had become the 26th country to take part in the games.

schema.headline: Uganda pulling out of Prince Harry's Invictus Games

title: Air traffic failure was avoidable, says transport secretary
description: A technical failure of the UK's air traffic control system that has caused widespread flight chaos was avoidable, according to the Transport Secretary
body: A technical failure of the UK's air traffic control system that has caused widespread flight chaos was avoidable, according to the Transport Secretary.  Heidi Alexander told the Commons she had ordered an independent investigation by the aviation watchdog into the system operated by Nats, which went down for four hours on Tuesday.More than 2,000 flights have been cancelled as disruption continued for a second day with passengers stuggling to fly out of and into the UK.After meeting with the boss of Nats, Martin Rolfe, Alexander said a cyberattack could be ruled out, but she added: "I do not believe this issue was unavoidable."Nats has apologised for its third major technical fault in three years.Alexander said she discussed with Rolfe how Nats, which is 49% owned by the government, "responded to resolve and minimise the disruption as quickly as possible".She said there had to be "tough questions about resilience of Nats systems", adding: "We also need to think about consumer redress issues."Earlier on Wednesday the government said it had confidence in Rolfe, who has led Nats for 11 years as airlines such as Wizz Air and Ryanair called for him to step down.Nats has been asked to investigate the incident and report back in one week. But Alexander said she has also asked the Civil Aviation Authority to conduct an independent review and present an update in six months' time.Airlines UK, which represents the country's carriers, said it had written to Alexander to "register serious concerns over yesterday's technical failure at Nats - the third major system failure in three years - which has caused major disruption across the UK's aviation network".Airlines UK's chief executive Tim Alderslade, said: "The result is a system where airlines pick up the bill for the mistakes of others, while the organisations responsible face little or no financial consequence."Accountability should sit where responsibility lies and the Civil Aviation Bill offers the opportunity to address this."The UK Civil Aviation Authority said passengers are unlikely to be entitled to compensation - though it reminded airlines of their responsibilities to look after passengers who flights had been delayed or cancelled.It added that the disruption caused by the Nats issue is "likely to be considered the result of 'extraordinary circumstances'", meaning passengers "are unlikely to be entitled to compensation for delays or cancellations that were directly caused by the incident."Nats first confirmed it was investigating a "technical issue" at 13:46 BST on Tuesday, "which is causing some disruption to flight departures". The glitch occurred at Nats' Swanwick Centre in Hampshire, where one of its two air traffic control centres are. The other is in Prestwick, Ayrshire.Around 90 minutes later, it said it had identified that the issue was with its flight processing system.This processes flight plans and other operational information used by controllers to manage air traffic.It continually updates flight information as aircraft progress through UK airspace, helping controllers maintain a safe and orderly flow of traffic.By 19:30, Nats said the system issue had been resolved and it was working to clear the backlog of flights.However, by Wednesday evening, the number of flights that had been cancelled or failed to take off since the fault first emerged had grown to more than 2,000, according to flight analytics firm Cirium.According to tracking site FlightRadar24, the worst affected airports were Heathrow, Gatwick, Manchester and Birmingham.A Heathrow spokesperson said on Wednesday its "operations are recovering"."Flights are operating today but we are expecting knock-on impacts as aircraft and crew reposition," it said.At Gatwick, a spokesperson said: "Flights have now resumed from London Gatwick. However, we still anticipate that it will take time for our operations to fully return to normal."Manchester, Luton, Stansted, Bristol, and Belfast City Airports all said on Wednesday that flights had resumed, though Bristol, Belfast and Luton said there continued to be knock-on effects.

schema.headline: Air traffic failure was avoidable, says transport secretary

title: Man charged with assisting Russian intelligence services
description: A 31-year-old British man has been charged under the National Security Act over alleged contact with Russia's military intelligence agency.Joshua Camm
body: A 31-year-old British man has been charged under the National Security Act over alleged contact with Russia's military intelligence agency.Joshua Cammidge, from Swindon, allegedly received instructions from an individual believed to be linked to the GRU Volunteer Corps, a group controlled by Russia's military intelligence agency, the Crown Prosecution service said.He has been charged with assisting a foreign intelligence service and preparatory conduct.He is due to appear at Westminster Magistrates' Court on Thursday.Cammidge was arrested at an address in Swindon on Friday by Counter Terrorism Policing (CTP) London officers, supported by officers from Wiltshire Police.He was taken to a London police station and searches were carried out at a different address in Swindon, the Metropolitan Police said.He was further arrested and detained under the National Security Act on Saturday.The force said he has been charged with assisting a foreign intelligence service contrary to Section 3 of the National Security Act 203 and preparatory conduct contrary to Section 18 of the National Security Act 2023.Frank Ferguson, chief crown prosecutor for the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) Special Crime and Counter Terrorism Division, said: "Our prosecutors have worked to establish that there is sufficient evidence to bring the case to court and that it is in the public interest to pursue criminal proceedings."We remind all concerned that proceedings against the defendant are active and he has the right to a fair trial."It is vital that there should be no reporting, commentary or sharing of information online which could in anyway prejudice these proceedings."Security Minister Dan Jarvis said: "The police have taken action against a potential threat, and I thank them for the vital work they do every day to keep us safe."Whilst it would be inappropriate to comment further on the specifics of this case, I know people will be concerned about recent incidents across Europe, intended to sow fear, create disruption and undermine support for Ukraine. They will not succeed."

schema.headline: Man charged with assisting Russian intelligence services

title: Tate brothers to remain in US custody as they fight extradition to UK
description: Andrew and Tristan Tate have lost their bid to be released from a Florida jail as they fight potential extradition to the UK to face charges of rape a
body: Andrew and Tristan Tate have lost their bid to be released from a Florida jail as they fight potential extradition to the UK to face charges of rape and trafficking.A federal judge in Miami denied them bail, saying the dual US-UK citizens' wealth and frequent international travel "constitute quintessential flight risks".US authorities have held them in custody since their July arrest in Miami, after the UK's Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) unveiled new charges against them.The UK has until 16 September to submit a full extradition request.They are facing a total of 59 charges in the UK, including rape and counts relating to sex trafficking and indecent images of a child.CPS originally brought 21 charges, but added 38 more in July for alleged actions spanning between 2010 and 2017.US authorities took the men into custody in July after the UK announced the new charges.The brothers also faced sex-trafficking charges in Romania in 2022, and were under a travel ban until they were allowed to come to the US in 2025. Several prominent US politicians, including Florida's Republican Governor Ron DeSantis, objected to the Tate brothers' arrival in the US.The brothers have denied all charges and allegations.Wednesday's decision means the brothers will remain jailed during what could be a lengthy extradition process.US Magistrate Judge Lauren Louis ruled that while the Tates "may not in fact possess what extravagant holdings they portray themselves as possessing online, the record reflects that they possess an exceptional capacity to flee the jurisdiction".The brothers' lawyers had argued that they had complied with the terms of their release while facing charges earlier in the UK and Romania.At a hearing on their potential release in August, Andrew Tate said he had "never committed the crimes I'm accused of."Tristan Tate described his detention conditions as small and hot, with little access to sunlight and exercise, and said he had lost 14 pounds (6.4kg)."It's beginning to grate on me because I can't partake in helping with my defence," he said, according to CBS News, the BBC's US partner. The British Embassy had asked the judge to keep the Tates in custody as the UK sought extradition, writing in court filings that the brothers were "flight risks" and claiming they "would interfere with witnesses if released".

schema.headline: Tate brothers to remain in US custody as they fight extradition to UK

title: Miliband rejects chief rabbi's claim British Jews in greater danger after sanctions move
description: Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband has rejected the chief rabbi's warning that British Jews are at greater risk after the UK announced sanctions on Israeli
body: Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband has rejected the chief rabbi's warning that British Jews are at greater risk after the UK announced sanctions on Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank.Miliband said that as a "proud British Jew" he disagreed with UK Chief Rabbi Sir Ephraim Mirvis, who described the move as a "truly dark day" that would "succeed only in bolstering the very extremism they seek to target"."We all need to do more to tackle antisemitism," Miliband said, "but I believe we can do that and stand up for British values".The sanctions on trade with illegal settlements in the occupied West Bank come against a backdrop of rising antisemitic incidents across the UK.The Community Security Trust (CST), an organisation that provides security support to the Jewish community, recorded 1,926 incidents of anti-Jewish hate across the UK in the first six months of 2026, a 21% increase on the same period in 2025.Prime Minister Andy Burnham defended his government's decision, telling MPs that "Britain has to stand for fairness against injustice". "Where people are being bullied out of their homes... we will always stand with the underdog," he said.The Palestinian presidency welcomed the UK's decision, saying it was "an important step towards confronting Israel's colonial system and its violations against the Palestinian people".There has been mixed reaction within the UK Jewish community on the sanctions and possible implications for security.The chief rabbi called the government's announcement "little more than political flag bearing for mendacious anti-Israel rhetoric".Sir Ephraim said: "Gesture politics of this kind feeds into an increasingly hostile discourse about Israel, and the cumulative effect of such punitive policies is to further embolden those, at home and abroad, who use hatred as a weapon against Jews."Asked about Mirvis's comments, Miliband said: "I don't agree with the chief rabbi, somebody... of whom I have great respect."He told BBC Radio 4's Today programme that "anyone who holds British Jews - or indeed Jews around the world - responsible for the actions of the Israeli government, is engaging in antisemitism, pure and simple".Meanwhile, the Jewish Leadership Council (JLC) warned the government's decision "risks becoming a de facto boycott of Israel" and accused Miliband of "yielding to pressure from the most extreme elements of British society".The Board of Deputies of British Jews said the decision to make the announcement before Rosh Hashanah - the Jewish New Year festival which begins on Friday - brings "concerns for communal security at their highest levels... felt particularly acutely by British Jews".It added that the deteriorating relationship between the UK and Israel has the potential to "further inflame community tensions here too", while also noting it had warned the Israeli government over the "intolerable settler violence" that harms Israel's reputation.Greater Manchester Police (GMP) announced on Wednesday that extra resources would be allocated during the Jewish High Holy Days to provide "extra visibility and security" and "ensure everyone can celebrate this time safely".Ch Supt Dave Meeney said: "Our officers will continue working with Jewish communities as we head into this important period for their faith, which we understand is a time which may bring heightened concern for the community."The sanctions have caused a diplomatic row with Israel which has closed the British consulate in East Jerusalem and banned 11 MPs and a campaigner from the country. On Wednesday, Israel's Diaspora Minister Amichai Chikli wrote to the head of Israeli border control recommending that several other British linked organisations and individuals should be refused entry to Israel.The list includes Oxfam, Save the Children, Norwegian Refugee Council, Islamic Relief Worldwide, and Medical Aid for Palestinians.Announcing the sanctions in the Commons on Tuesday, Miliband said the "new approach" was needed because of the plans for the E1 development - a controversial settlement project that would effectively cut off the occupied West Bank from East Jerusalem and divide the territory in two.He also told MPs that the UK agreed there was ethnic cleansing in areas of the occupied West Bank - accusing "settler terrorists" of driving Palestinians from their land."And all too often, the Israeli government has turned a blind eye to this," Miliband said.The sanctions will target companies and people providing services like construction and financing of settlements. There will also be a ban on the advertising illegal settlements in the UK. Miliband said the measures could take up to nine months to put in place. Canada and France have also banned goods from the settlements as part of a co-ordinated action with allies.

schema.headline: Miliband rejects chief rabbi's claim British Jews in greater danger after sanctions move

title: RNLI volunteer targeted online and branded ‘traitor’ after Portsmouth protests
description: ByMarco Silva, Benedict Garman and Adam DurbinBBC VerifyAn RNLI volunteer who was targeted with abuse online after being wrongly identified as having
body: ByMarco Silva, Benedict Garman and Adam DurbinBBC VerifyAn RNLI volunteer who was targeted with abuse online after being wrongly identified as having helped small boat migrants reach land in Portsmouth has told BBC Verify he is not a "traitor".Neil and his colleagues were filmed wearing their lifesaving gear on a lifeboat by anti-migrant activists near the harbour on Sunday night, after hundreds of protesters descended on the area and shut down roads in response to dozens of asylum seekers being brought to shore.The lifeboat crew's images were later used in posts accusing them of assisting what some users on X described as "an invasion", several of which also called for them to be "named and shamed".These posts, which were collectively viewed at least two million times, also incorrectly claimed Neil and another colleague were two entirely different RNLI crew members whose names were available online.Figure caption, Lifeboat volunteer branded 'traitor' after anti-migrant protestsNeil, whose face was visible in the video, told BBC Verify that the RNLI vessel was in the area to illuminate the beach "purely for the safety of the protesters" who had entered the sea. "I am not a traitor," he added.Replies to the most widely shared posts featured wide-ranging abuse, including suggestions they should be refused service at pubs and to track down their families.At least one post has since been removed for violating X's rules. The platform has been approached for comment.Neil has been an RNLI volunteer for over a decade and said that despite the abuse he was undeterred and would continue to head out to rescue people when needed."I'll be back on the boat when the pager goes off," he said, adding: "It'd just be nice for those people who call me a traitor to know that I'm not a traitor. I'm just a volunteer crew."BBC Verify is not sharing the full names of anyone mentioned in the posts, or the RNLI crews they volunteer with, to protect their identities.Image source, PA MediaImage caption, Neil told BBC Verify his lifeboat was in the area as a safeguard after some protesters entered the seaAsked about the online abuse in Parliament on Tuesday, Digital Secretary Lisa Nandy told MPs she had spoken with tech companies about how the names, addresses and photographs of RNLI staff and volunteers were reportedly shared online.Nandy also said that both she and the government are "concerned" about the risks posed to adults and children from doxxing - the term used to describe people whose private information has been shared online without their consent.Dr Anna Tippett, a criminologist and cyber-vigilantism researcher at the University of Hertfordshire, told BBC Verify doxxing can create a "profound sense of vulnerability", as the "boundary between online abuse and potential offline harm becomes increasingly difficult to judge".She added it is "particularly concerning when those targeted are volunteers", as concerns they or their families could be identified, threatened or abused "could discourage others from taking on these kinds of public-facing voluntary roles".

schema.headline: RNLI volunteer targeted online and branded ‘traitor’ after Portsmouth protests

title: Germany's Merz attacks AfD in parliament after far-right election win
description: German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has clashed with AfD leader Alice Weidel in parliament, calling her party a "destructive force" with a migration poli
body: German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has clashed with AfD leader Alice Weidel in parliament, calling her party a "destructive force" with a migration policy that amounts to "ethnic cleansing" for skilled workers.Merz was addressing the Bundestag in the aftermath of the anti-immigration party's sweeping victory in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt where it won almost 44% of the vote, while the chancellor's conservatives saw their vote halved.Weidel told MPs that voters had shown that Merz's coalition with the centre left was a total failure and his time was up.Merz hit back saying the AfD had harmed German interests by backing Russia, and its "remigration" policy would affect millions.It is not yet clear whether the party will be able to form a government or not in Saxony-Anhalt, having fallen three seats short of an outright majority. No far-right party has won power in any of Germany's 16 states since World War Two, and Merz has admitted the "seismic" result has changed Germany.The AfD's success has been praised by US President Donald Trump, who said "the Populist Party in Germany just had a really big night", linking the victory to "absolutely horrible immigration rules and regulations".The AfD in Saxony-Anhalt has been labelled as "right-wing extremist" by German domestic intelligence and the party has promised a "deportation and remigration" offensive targeting irregular migrants.Trump had been due to speak by phone to the German chancellor on Wednesday to mark the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 attacks in the US, but the government spokesman in Berlin said the call had been postponed without saying why. No new date has been set.As leader of the main opposition party in the Bundestag, Weidel opened the session by telling Merz his Christian Democrats had been "pulverised" in Saxony-Anhalt, after winning 17.2% of the vote, and she accused his government with the Social Democrats of driving Germany towards bankruptcy.Merz said her party had not won an outright majority in Saxony-Anhalt and it would not achieve one in Germany.  "You are and will remain a destructive force," he said, accusing the party of cheating the voters by saying before the election that their candidate for premier, Ulrich Siegmund, would only rule if he won a majority, but hours after the vote deciding to go and find one.The AfD has opened the door to working with another party, perhaps the left-wing populist BSW, as long as it backs Siegmund to be state premier.Siegmund's number two in Saxony-Anhalt, has even suggested that Merz's CDU could work with his party, if it abandons the so-called firewall (Brandmauer), under which no mainstream party will work with the far right.

schema.headline: Germany's Merz attacks AfD in parliament after far-right election win

title: 'Constantly on my mind' - 9/11 agony endures for bereaved, 25 years on
description: Image source, Tom RestaImage caption, John Resta and his wife SylviaByAlice CuddyThe US government has described it as the "most egregious criminal ac
body: Image source, Tom RestaImage caption, John Resta and his wife SylviaByAlice CuddyThe US government has described it as the "most egregious criminal act on American soil in modern history".But a quarter of a century on, the trial of its alleged mastermind is yet to begin and families of those killed fear that time for justice to be delivered is running out.Tom Resta's brother John and his wife Sylvia, who was seven months pregnant, were among the almost 3,000 people killed on 11 September 2001 when hijackers flew planes into the World Trade Center in New York City and the Pentagon in Virginia. Another crashed in a field in Pennsylvania after the passengers fought back.The couple had been preparing their unborn baby's nursery, painting it with characters from the children's television show Blue's Clues in the days before 9/11. They had dreamed of having a baby and doted on the children of friends and family.On the day of the attacks, the couple - both traders - were working on the 92nd floor of the north tower of the World Trade Center."After all this time, it still chokes me up," Resta told the BBC through tears. While 25 years have passed, he said 9/11 was "almost constantly" on his mind.Resta has been to the US naval base of Guantanamo Bay four times to watch complex pre-trial proceedings for alleged 9/11 mastermind Khalid Sheikh Mohammed and his co-defendants - a process he describes as "laborious and tedious".A military prison was established on the base in south-eastern Cuba during the "war on terror" that followed the 9/11 attacks, and Mohammed - often referred to as KSM - has now been held there for 20 years without ever being convicted.Relatives of victims enter a lottery process to attend the proceedings in a high-security courtroom, where thick glass separates them and members of the press from the defendants.The pre-trial process has been going on for so long that it has now been presided over by five different military judges.Last month, as the 25th anniversary approached, there was a flurry of movement and something of a breakthrough, with a trial date set for Mohammed for June 2028.But Resta said he was bracing himself for further delays, and with so much time having passed, some of his relatives feared they would not live long enough to see the trial."My father will be 98 in November, and I don't think he's expecting to see it. I have a lot of family members - aunts, uncles - that would all like to see it happen. But my parents in particular, I don't think they expect to live long enough," he said."Hopefully all the defendants will still be alive by the time we get to trial. That's a big worry," he added.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, A tribute in light above the New York City skyline, at the 2024 anniversary Resta's concerns that a trial could still be further delayed were shared by relatives of other 9/11 victims.Earlier this year, Stephan Gerhardt made his sixth trip to Guantanamo. He said seeing convictions for the death of his younger brother Ralph was vital for him, but something he wished he no longer had to think about."I want to concentrate on the memories," he said.  "I still have Ralph's car. I'm trying to restore it and get it in pristine shape again… We were recently visiting my parents, and we found some of his things that they were holding onto, and the emotion behind it is like, 'yeah, this is just some old stuff, but it belonged to my little brother'."Gerhardt said his "biggest concern" was that he wanted to see Mohammed and his alleged co-conspirators convicted before they died."They're getting elderly… I don't want them to pass away without being convicted, because that would be an injustice to all the family members - that we captured these people, but we never got to try them and convict them for the mass murder that they did of our loved ones."Image source, FBIImage caption, Khalid Sheikh Mohammed as he appeared on the FBI's Most Wanted websiteMohammed has been charged with offences including conspiracy and murder, with 2,976 victims listed on the charge sheet. He is accused of conceiving the idea of training pilots to fly commercial planes into buildings and taking those plans to Osama bin Laden, leader of the militant Islamist group al-Qaeda.He has previously said he planned the "9/11 operation from A to Z".But days after the trial date was set for 2028, the military judge threw out confessions made by Mohammed to FBI agents on Guantanamo Bay after he was brought there from secret CIA prisons known as "black sites", which he had been held in for years. In his ruling, the judge described Mohammed's treatment by the CIA as "extraordinary physical and mental abuse".He said the confessions were not voluntary and could not be used against Mohammed at trial.Experts say the torture of Mohammed and his alleged co-conspirators has been the main reason for the lengthy delays in the case."Every single issue has been litigated through the issue of torture," said Kasey McCall-Smith, an international law professor at Edinburgh University.She said the defendants were subjected to "years of abuse", including waterboarding and stress positions.Image source, Tom RestaImage caption, John and Sylvia Resta on their wedding dayJohn Ryan, author of America's Trial: Torture and the 9/11 Case on Guantanamo Bay, said last month's ruling means prosecutors lose what they had described as their best evidence against Mohammed, but it is unclear how much it will impact the case.The prosecution has other evidence, Ryan says, including intercepted phone calls and secret recordings, but whether they can feature in the trial is not yet guaranteed. "Mohammad's team and the other defence teams will file motions to suppress some of these categories of evidence, as well."During the George W Bush administration, the US admitted using "enhanced interrogation techniques" to acquire information from suspects but said these methods saved lives and never amounted to torture. President Barack Obama banned them on his second day in office.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, President George W Bush on Air Force One after the attacksRelatives of the victims say the torture of the defendants has so far blocked their right to justice."If we would've not tortured them, the legal implications here would've been much, much simpler. They probably would've been sentenced to death a long time ago," said Gerhardt. "I can't control what the government did, and we've got to live with the impacts."Both Gerhardt and Resta travelled to Guantanamo in early 2025 when Mohammed and two of his co-defendants had been due to plead guilty under a controversial deal struck with US government prosecutors, through which they would not face a death penalty trial.The BBC was with them at the base when the pleas were paused at the last minute after the US government argued that to "deprive the government and the American people of a public trial as to the respondents' guilt and the possibility of capital punishment" would cause "irreparable" harm.Legal wrangling over the validity of the deal is continuing.Some victims' relatives viewed the deal as the only way through, while others criticised it as too lenient and lacking transparency.Resta said he had supported the deal to secure convictions."My philosophy is these guys are not the kind of people that should be out walking the streets, but as far as I'm concerned, they can just stay right where they are.  I just want them convicted," he said.Brett Eagleson, whose dad Bruce was killed in the attacks, said he wanted a full trial, not a plea deal."It's not so much that I'm taking an opinion on life or death for these prisoners, but I believe in the judicial system and I believe that the process works and I believe that a trial and discovery and sort of a public airing is the way to flush the truth out," he said.Image source, Brett EaglesonImage caption, Brett Eagleson was 15 when his father Bruce was killed Eagleson described the situation on Guantanamo as "a mess" and said he had decided not to attend any of the pre-trial proceedings there."My overall feeling is a sense of betrayal from the US government and a sense of extreme frustration," he said. "They've botched every single part of this trial."With 25 years having passed since the attacks, he said that while 9/11 was a constant presence in his own life, to the wider public it was "becoming a historical event"."I think people just assume that we got Bin Laden, we're out of Iraq, the war in Afghanistan's over, and they just assume that chapter has ended."When the trial does eventually start, at a military court at Guantanamo, it has been estimated that it will last about a year.Professor Kasey McCall-Smith said the point of the pre-trial proceedings had been determining "what evidence gets in and what evidence doesn't get in"."If that is agreed in advance, the trial can be more expeditious," she explained.As the relatives of the victims prepared for another anniversary marking the death of their loved ones, Gerhardt said he was looking forward to a time that the trial was over and he no longer had to think about or travel to Guantanamo."It's a place I don't want to come back to. I want to live my life, enjoy my passions and my memories of Ralph," he said.

schema.headline: 'Constantly on my mind' - 9/11 agony endures for bereaved, 25 years on

title: 'It's been a nightmare': Passengers face airport chaos after UK air traffic issue
description: Passengers left stranded by an hours-long air traffic control issue at UK airports have told the BBC of nightmare delays, chaotic scenes and waylaid h
body: Passengers left stranded by an hours-long air traffic control issue at UK airports have told the BBC of nightmare delays, chaotic scenes and waylaid holiday plans.Hundreds of thousands of people are thought to have been hit with flight cancellations and delays throughout Tuesday and Wednesday after a technical problem caused the air traffic outage.That included newlyweds Sasha and James, who told BBC Your Voice they spent three hours stranded in Wetherspoons at Gatwick after their flight to their honeymoon was cancelled.Some also described sleeping on airport floors and chaos at baggage reclaim as thousands looked to reorganise their plans, while others have been stranded abroad while trying to get back to the UK.Nats, the UK's air traffic control provider, has said flight operations are now stable but airlines have warned of continued knock-on disruption. Passengers have been advised to check their flight status before travelling to airports.The boss of Nats Martin Rolfe apologised for the disruption and also met with Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander on Wednesday, who asked for a full investigation.Most of the UK's main airports were hit by the problem including Heathrow, Gatwick, Luton and Glasgow.Speaking to the BBC earlier on Wednesday, newly married couple Sasha and James Graham said they were boarding their flight from Gatwick to Funchal on the island of Madeira when they were "turned right back around".Phil White also spoke of incredibly busy scenes in the airport's baggage reclaim hall, describing it as "carnage" as an influx of disrupted passengers tried to find their luggage."All the bags from every cancelled flight were sent to one reclaim carousel. So there were a thousand or so people trying to get close enough to get their cases," he said."The baggage hall was the worst and they're very lucky that there wasn't any sort of incident as tempers frayed and the concourse was getting hotter."Elsewhere, people spoke of spending the night on the floors of airports and hotels across the globe when flights back into the UK were cancelled.Sukie Perera, from Cardiff, describing her experience of being stuck in Turkey said "it has been a nightmare" and communication at the airport was poor.She won't be able to fly home until Thursday but joked that at least "the view is beautiful".Paul Willows, currently in Rhodes, Greece, with his family said they had to sleep on the floor of a hotel's conference room on Tuesday night.He said: "They stripped all the cushions off the sunbeds and laid them in the conference room. I dare say there were about 80 of us on the floor."Despite it having "not been a comfortable night at all", Paul said there was a "good element of pulling together" from those impacted.Alan Jones and Kelly Fewery also said their family was "absolutely exhausted" after sleeping on the floor of Dalaman Airport in Turkey without blankets or pillows.

schema.headline: 'It's been a nightmare': Passengers face airport chaos after UK air traffic issue

title: Andy Burnham: National security can't come at expense of social security
description: Andy Burnham has said national security "can't come at the expense of social security", as he was challenged over funding for defence at Prime Ministe
body: Andy Burnham has said national security "can't come at the expense of social security", as he was challenged over funding for defence at Prime Minister's Questions.Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch pressed Burnham over whether he would spend 3% of GDP on defence by 2030 and how he would pay for this.The PM said the government's commitment to defence was "absolute" and he would set a target date to reach the 3% figure in the spring.Burnham said he would fund defence and get the welfare bill down in "the Labour way", by changing education, supporting young people and providing more mental health support.The Conservatives seized on the comments, with a party spokesperson saying: "Britain heard it loud and clear today: Andy Burnham will not cut welfare to fund the defence of our country."The prime minister is prioritising the ballooning benefits bill over our national security. Shameful."After PMQs, Burnham's team was at pains to stress his commitment that "national security is the most important duty of any government", and stressed the prime minister had been "consistent about getting the welfare bill down". But they said that did not mean "crude cuts" that could "put people into crisis" by making them homeless and so creating higher costs elsewhere in the system to support them.In the Commons session, Burnham repeated that the government would meet the Nato target of spending 3.5% of GDP on defence by 2035, with a target date for hitting the 3% figure set out in the spending review in the spring.The PM said he had appointed John Healey, who resigned as Sir Keir Starmer's defence secretary over the government's failure to commit to a 3% increase by 2030, "because of his strong commitment to the defence of this nation".However, Badenoch hit back that 2035 was "a decade away" and "the threats are now".She questioned whether Burnham was "unable" or "just unwilling" to meet the 2030 target.In response, Burnham insisted: "This chancellor of all chancellors will be willing to provide that funding to our armed forces."However, he rejected a Conservative plan to partly fund increased defence spending by saving at least £4bn through reforms to housing benefit."I don't think, myself, that taking £4bn out of housing benefit is going to get the right consensus around this issue because that would create levels of homelessness in this country... that we wouldn't have seen before, hundreds of thousands of children in temporary accommodation," he said."Yes, we do everything to support our national security, but it can't come at the expense of social security."He added: "This side of the House will not be forced to choose between the two and we will set out a plan to get to 3.5% by 2035 at the spending review."Badenoch said Burnham's comments were "unbelievable", adding: "We need to fund our defence, not spend all of our money on welfare."Burnham insisted he would "bring the welfare budget down" by tackling the number of young people not in education, employment or training."That's the Labour way to get the welfare bill down," he said."That is the right way to fund defence."Badenoch accused Burnham of being "continuity Keir"."He's pretending that he's the change candidate. But the fact is, he's still failing to cut welfare," she said.As prime minister, Sir Keir attempted to cut disability benefits but was forced to row back on the plans in the face of opposition from Labour MPs.Cutting the welfare bill is a key part of Tory proposals for funding increased defence spending.Spending on benefits has ballooned in recent years and is forecast to rise to £408.6bn in 2030/31, according to figures from the Department for Work and Pensions.There is particular concern about the nearly one million young people in the UK who are not in education, employment or training – known as "Neets".The government has asked former minister Alan Milburn to look into the issue and he is expected to publish his final recommendations for how to tackle the problem shortly.

schema.headline: Andy Burnham: National security can't come at expense of social security

title: Google to fund Finnish AI with €13bn investment and nuclear power pact
description: Google will buy up to half the electricity produced by one of Finland's nuclear power plants as part of a record €13bn (£11bn; $15bn) investment in th
body: Google will buy up to half the electricity produced by one of Finland's nuclear power plants as part of a record €13bn (£11bn; $15bn) investment in the country's AI infrastructure, the company announced.The US tech giant said the package would fund three new data centres, expand an existing site and support energy projects to power growing demand for AI services."This is Google's largest single investment in Europe and a testament to Finland's leadership in responsibly building AI infrastructure," the company said on Wednesday."Google's decision is a clear testament to our strengths," Finland's Prime Minister Petteri Orpo said in a statement.As part of the deal, Google signed a 22-year contract with Finnish utility Fortum to buy up to 50% of the output from the Loviisa nuclear power plant.Earlier this week, TikTok announced a $1bn investment in Finland to build a new data centre in Kouvola, pointing to the country's "strong digital infrastructure, clean energy mix, robust data governance and skilled tech talent".    Finland has emerged as an attractive location for data centres because of its cool climate, plentiful low-carbon electricity and relatively uncongested power grid. The colder temperatures can reduce the energy needed to cool facilities packed with computer servers.Technology companies are racing to secure power supplies as the AI boom drives demand for vast networks of data centres.The Google investment is expected to support more than 37,000 jobs during construction and boost Finland's GDP by €3.6bn a year, according to Google. Construction is set to take place in 2027 and 2028."The value of the data economy extends far beyond direct investment into spurring innovation, research and development," Orpo added. "Deepening our collaboration with Google will deliver lasting benefits for both parties."Google will build new data centres in Kajaani, Muhos and Vaala, while expanding its existing facility in Hamina, which it established after converting a former paper mill in 2009.The infrastructure will help support products such as its AI chatbot Gemini, alongside services including Search, Maps and YouTube.Google said the investments also covered "clean energy projects, and dedicated nature and community funds to support local biodiversity, education, research, and workforce development"."Google is proud to deepen our roots in Finland," said Ruth Porat, president and chief investment officer of Alphabet and Google."This investment underscores Google's commitment to grow our presence responsibly, pairing the expansion of our technical infrastructure with new energy capacity, grid enhancements, and energy affordability initiatives," she added.Earlier this year, Google's parent company Alphabet raised its global spending plans to as much as $205bn as it sought to expand computing capacity for AI services.The agreement with Fortum provides long-term financial certainty for the Loviisa plant, which currently generates about 10% of Finland's electricity.Fortum said Google's commitment would support an investment programme aimed at extending the life of the nuclear station and increasing its generating capacity.

schema.headline: Google to fund Finnish AI with €13bn investment and nuclear power pact

title: Police launch criminal investigation into Reform UK donations
description: The Metropolitan Police is carrying out a criminal investigation into Reform UK over allegations it broke foreign funding laws, following a broadcast
body: The Metropolitan Police is carrying out a criminal investigation into Reform UK over allegations it broke foreign funding laws, following a broadcast by Channel 4 News last week.An undercover reporter recorded two senior Reform aides apparently suggesting a way around electoral law to secure foreign party donations, one of which would have totalled £500,000.The police investigation by the Met's Special Enquiry Team is being folded into an inquiry that has been under way into other donations to the party.A Reform UK spokesman said the party "denies any wrongdoing and will fully cooperate with the investigation". "We won't be commenting further while a live investigation is under way."A Met spokesperson said it had received "a number of reports relating to donations and polling involving a political party", after the film by Channel 4 News and Verbatim Investigations was shown on Thursday evening. In its statement, the Met Police said: "All allegations under investigation relate to potential offences under the Political Parties, Elections and Referendums Act 2000.""Detectives continue to liaise closely with the Electoral Commission and Crown Prosecution Service as enquiries progress."The police spokesperson said detectives were seeking to obtain footage relating to the broadcast.The film overshadowed the party's conference in Birmingham and led to the party losing two key figures - Dan Jukes, chief of staff to the leader Nigel Farage, and James Orr, head of policy.In the news report, an undercover investigator posing as the son of an American donor is recorded raising a concern that his father wouldn't be able to directly donate to the party within the law.Electoral law states that to be a permissible donor to a UK political party you must be a UK registered voter, or a company registered in the UK.Jukes appears to suggest that the donation could be in the UK-based son's name, although the money would have come from his American father.Elsewhere, James Orr, the party's head of policy suggests that the father could pay for opinion polling to support one of Reform's campaigns.Farage and Jukes were also filmed at a lunch in Clacton where it is suggested the US donor, who was being played by an actor, gives £500,000 to Reform through his son.Farage told the BBC he "frankly wasn't listening" to the discussion about the potential donation. Channel 4 News has said the payment was never made. He dismissed the comments made by his aide in the film as "loose pub talk including a couple of boasts that simply were not true".Jukes has denied "any wrongdoing" and said he had "stepped back from politics in order to clear my name".Last week, Orr told Sky News he would cooperate with the party's internal investigation "fully".The Met had already been investigating whether payments to Reform in the weeks before the last election complied with donation laws.The probe is examining donations given directly to the party by Fiona Cottrell, mother of longstanding Nigel Farage ally, George Cottrell.It is also examining payments from a company controlled by Reform's deputy leader Richard Tice, which received £1m from Fiona Cottrell in June 2024.A Verbatim Investigations spokesperson said: "Verbatim will cooperate with the police's investigation."Labour Party Chair Bridget Phillipson said: "Farage needs to wake up and realise the buck stops with him."Reform's failure to take responsibility for their actions shows just how unfit they are for office."The Liberal Democrat's Cabinet Office spokeswoman Lisa Smart said: "Every Reform MP urgently needs to state whether they or their campaigns have benefited from any foreign money."Zack Polanski, leader of the Green Party in England and Wales, said: "Nigel Farage and Lee Anderson hoped they could pin all this on two of their most senior advisors, but they have more questions to answer about how much they knew."

schema.headline: Police launch criminal investigation into Reform UK donations

title: Police say Nottingham attacks were 'not preventable', public inquiry hears
description: A police force has said the Nottingham attacks were not "reasonably foreseeable or preventable", a public inquiry has heard.Valdo Calocane - who was d
body: A police force has said the Nottingham attacks were not "reasonably foreseeable or preventable", a public inquiry has heard.Valdo Calocane - who was diagnosed with paranoid schizophrenia in 2020 - stabbed to death Barnaby Webber, Grace O'Malley-Kumar and Ian Coates, and tried to kill three others in a spate of attacks on 13 June 2023.Nottinghamshire Police dealt with Calocane on 10 or 11 occasions between 2020 and 2022, but John Beggs KC - representing the force - said police "cannot manage dangerous paranoid schizophrenics". At the Nottingham Inquiry, external - which has been examining the attacks - Beggs challenged the idea that any police mistakes before the killings were missed opportunities.Calocane admitted three counts of manslaughter on the grounds of diminished responsibility, and three counts of attempted murder.Following Calocane's sentencing to a hospital order in January 2024, a series of failings by authorities emerged, including the police, which led to calls by the affected families for a statutory public inquiry.The judge-led inquiry began in February this year, and laid bare the extent of failings in Calocane's care and his previous interactions with police, including the failure to execute an arrest warrant for Calocane, which was still outstanding at the time of the attacks. The inquiry, which is being led by retired senior judge Deborah Taylor KC, is in its second day of closing submissions.Addressing Taylor on Wednesday, Beggs said: "We respectfully invite you to avoid the mindset that a mistake or an omission by an officer represents a missed opportunity to prevent this tragedy."The appropriate question might be - missed opportunity to do what precisely?"The police cannot manage dangerous paranoid schizophrenics."Nottinghamshire Police has maintained throughout its evidence that if the warrant had been executed, it was unlikely to have prevented the attacks from happening."The criticism of our failure to execute that warrant is entirely justified," Beggs said."What isn't justified is the assumption that that failure represented a missed opportunity to prevent the attacks."That view has been disputed by the bereaved families, including their legal representative, Tim Moloney KC, who previously said any attempt to suggest arresting Calocane would not have made a difference would be "cowardly and insulting".Beggs said a "low-level to high-level community order, we suggest is the likely outcome". Some members of the bereaved families left the hearing room as Beggs continued.The inquiry evidence previously revealed that between 2020 and 2023 - after Calocane had become unwell - he was involved in a number of incidents of violence and aggression, including breaking into his neighbours' homes, assaulting his housemates and attacking a police officer. In May 2020, Calocane - who is being referred to throughout the inquiry as VC - broke into the flat of a woman, minutes after being released by police following an earlier incident. The woman, known to the inquiry as Feven, fell from a first-floor window in an attempt to escape, was left with a fractured spine, and required surgery.  On Tuesday, the inquiry heard Nottinghamshire Police had not disclosed the discovery of documents found in a bin at Calocane's address, which contained a list of explosives, until June this year.On the documents, Calocane wrote bullet points on one page about explosives under the heading "thoughts", including TNT and nitrate fertiliser.The inquiry heard they had not been made available by police to the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) or to psychiatric experts.The inquiry heard further violent assaults by Calocane on colleagues at warehouses in Nottinghamshire were also not disclosed to the inquiry team until after the public hearings had taken place.This included an assault on a colleague in a warehouse in Eastwood in 2021 and another in Normanton in February 2023.Continuing his evidence on Wednesday, Beggs said: "All of the interactions with the police and VC from my constabulary were borne of mental illness." He added there was "no escalation of VC's behaviour" and that the incidents of him breaking into neighbours' homes showed "no evidence of his intention to hurt anyone".However, when challenged by Taylor, Beggs said VC hurting someone was a "possibility". Beggs added: "Whilst shortcomings by individual Nottinghamshire officers in specific incidents have been identified and largely accepted by those officers, either in their statements or in their live evidence, the June attacks were not reasonably foreseeable or preventable on the information known to Nottinghamshire Police."Beggs was also challenged by inquiry chairwoman Taylor on the absence of an apology on behalf of the police to the families affected in his closing submissions."If an apology had not been proffered which I had not appreciated then I proffer it on behalf of my client," Beggs added.Beggs also addressed Nottinghamshire Police's response on the day of the attacks. In evidence, the inquiry heard how there was a lack of communication between officers on the day of the attacks, and how the bereaved families waited hours for confirmation that their loved ones had been killed. The initial attacks on Barnaby and Grace were also assumed by the force incident manager at the time as a "robbery".Ian's body, the inquiry heard, was left at the scene for about 15 hours. A forensic tent had not arrived at the scene where Ian died to cover his body for more than two hours.Addressing inquiry chairwoman Taylor, Beggs said: "On 13 June, Nottinghamshire officers and staff attended the scenes of the carnage inflicted by VC quickly and they managed the victims and the evidential scenes well." Challenging Beggs, Taylor said: "Well just a moment there - what about the evidential scene with Ian Coates and what happened there? Would you say that was well managed?""Overall it was well-managed," Beggs replied.Taylor said: "The fact that he was there for 12 to 15 hours for that?"Beggs went on to say the force was "not saying it was perfect", but added "no evidential degradation was suffered as a result of delay". The inquiry also heard evidence of misconduct by police officers and staff in the aftermath of the attacks, including inappropriate access to the case and digital evidence.Two officers were also disciplined for sharing insensitive WhatsApp messages about the attacks.The force acknowledged it failed to deliver information to the families in a "consistent, clear and timely manner" and failed in its management of misconduct. Beggs added: "However, fair and objective analysis of the evidence shows that there was no attempt, however much the media may report it, by senior officers to cover up any matters from the bereaved or survivors of the public."He also highlighted the demand on the police and the mental healthcare system in his closing submissions.Beggs said when policing was "running hot all the time, the risks of things going wrong increases". He added: "We respectfully observe that there is little point this inquiry making recommendations that create further demand on the services which struggled to cope with existing demand, and unless new money is injected into policing and/or mental health services, the current mental health crisis will continue."James Berry KC, representing Leicestershire Police, told the inquiry three officers made a "series of errors" when responding to reports that Calocane had assaulted two warehouse workers at Arvarto, in Kegworth, in May 2023.The officers' failure to identify that a warrant was out for Calocane's arrest was a "missed opportunity" to inform Nottinghamshire Police of his latest offence, he said.He argued that, despite the errors, it is "far from clear" if a report to the neighbouring force would have prompted Calocane's arrest, due to Nottinghamshire Police's failure to carry out the warrant for several months.Concluding his statement, Berry said any recommendations made by the inquiry to the police would only be effective if they were backed by "new government funding".Leicestershire Police already has "insufficient resources to meet the demand they face", he added.During evidence, the CPS was questioned about how it came to the decision to accept Calocane's guilty pleas of manslaughter on the grounds of diminished responsibility.In her closing submission, Jacqueline Carey KC, representing the CPS, said it was the "correct legal decision"."I say legal decision, because it was one for the CPS and the CPS alone, and it was a decision to take impartially, dispassionately and most important of all, independently," she added.The families affected previously described "unfolding horror" as they were informed about the decision to accept Calocane's plea. They also believed the decision was rushed, not fully informed and that the details provided to them were not clear enough. Carey said Calocane was in a "psychotic state" when he carried out the killings and attacked survivors Sharon Miller, Wayne Birkett and Marcin Gawronski.She added: "This is such a clear diminished responsibility case for so many reasons. I think it's very difficult to see how experts could have reached any other conclusion in this case."Taylor will have until May to complete a final report on her findings and make any recommendations. In her closing remarks, Taylor said she intended to stick to the agreed timeframe for publication of the report, and reminded the participants of their obligation to correct any omissions or mistakes in their evidence before 31 December.She added: "For those most closely affected by these terrible events, bereaved families who have worked so hard to achieve the inquiry and the survivors who have borne the weight of it all as it's revealed day by day, you have no such obligations, and I hope that these few months will give you much-needed time for reflection and healing and gathering strength for the publication of the report and what may then follow."

schema.headline: Police say Nottingham attacks were 'not preventable', public inquiry hears

title: Dallas Cowboys Cheerleader Reece Weaver swaps boots for Broadway
description: Former Dallas Cowboys Cheerleader Reece Weaver has shelved her cowboy boots and swapped the football pitch for the stage as she steps into one of the
body: Former Dallas Cowboys Cheerleader Reece Weaver has shelved her cowboy boots and swapped the football pitch for the stage as she steps into one of the most famous roles in the world. Weaver was a breakout star of the Netflix docuseries America's Sweethearts: Dallas Cowboys Cheerleaders, with her exit from the squad a major storyline of the third season. Making her Broadway debut in the musical Chicago, she faced criticism that it was her profile, more than her talent, which landed her the role. After much fan speculation, she officially stepped into the role of murderess Roxie Hart this week at New York's Ambassador Theatre."The audience loved her," says Sealy Sikes, who attended the opening night with her mum Tammy Pack.Her mum's a big fan of the Netflix series, which follows the cheerleaders through gruelling auditions and training regimes as they compete for their spot dancing in one of the world's best known squads.Sikes says she was less familiar with fan favourite Weaver before the curtain went up and was impressed with how she commanded the stage."She did a great job, she's a very big, charismatic actor."It was a little bit shaky at the beginning, but if I wasn't hyper aware that it was her first time, I wouldn't have even thought anything about it." Clips shared on social media showed the audience erupting in applause for a grinning Weaver as she took her first bow.Chicago's choice of Weaver isn't the first time a production has picked a celebrity star. Earlier this year, rapper Megan Thee Stallion was cast as Zidler in Moulin Rouge!, becoming the first woman to play the role of the nightclub boss.Although she quit the show early, her performance received strong reviews and boosted interest in the show, with fans reportedly travelling from across the US, external to see her. Six The Musical also booked Grammy-winning singer Abigail Barlow and content creator Dylan Mulvaney for a run of shows back in January. "When a show starts to struggle a little bit more, they tend to use celebrity casting," says Boucher. "By being there, they're actually keeping a lot of other people employed at the same time."Reece's role has already attracted her fans to Broadway, with some like Samantha Milo waiting to meet her at the theatre's stage door on her debut night. "I do think there is some stunt casting involved, however she is a great addition regardless," the 19-year-old tells Newsbeat. "She earned her spot there, she has been dancing and performing her whole life, this was a big goal for her.""Having Reece step into the role helps new fans who may never have thought to go and see Chicago, find a way to enjoy the show."The production runs for six weeks until 18 October. Additional reporting by Miya Chahal.

schema.headline: Dallas Cowboys Cheerleader Reece Weaver swaps boots for Broadway
